Long before you ever
held a crayon,
you may have already
picked a favorite hand.
The first hints show
up in ultrasound scans
of fetuses just ten
weeks into pregnancy.
So where does handedness
come from?
The answer turns out
to be stranger than
a single gene.
In ultrasound studies in
Belfast, about eighty-five
percent of fetuses at
ten weeks moved their
right arm more than
their left.
Later in pregnancy,
about ninety-five percent
were seen sucking their
right thumb.
The researchers then
followed some of these
children until they were
ten to twelve years old.
All sixty who had
sucked their right thumb
grew up right-handed.
Of the fifteen who
had sucked their left
thumb, ten became
left-handers.
For a long time,
scientists assumed that
hand preference starts
in the brain.
But a preference can
be seen from around
the eighth week of
pregnancy, before the motor
cortex is connected to
the spinal cord.
In 2017, a team
at Ruhr University Bochum
in Germany studied fetal
spinal cords from the
eighth to the twelfth week.
Genes were more active
on one side than
the other, in the
segments that control the
arms and legs.
Some of the genes
linked to left-handedness
help build microtubules,
tiny tubes that act
like a scaffold inside
our cells.
Related cell machinery
helps an early embryo
tell its left side
from its right,
which is why your
heart usually sits on
the left and your
liver on the right.
Scientists suspect this
same toolkit also plays
a part in which
hand we prefer.
So is there a
left-handed gene?
No.
When both parents are
left-handed, the chance
that their child will
be left-handed is only
about twenty-six percent.
Among identical twins,
who share essentially the
same DNA, roughly one
pair in five disagrees.
In 2019, Oxford researchers
scanned about four hundred
thousand genomes and found
a handful of regions.
None of them works
like a switch.
Each one only nudges
the odds a little.
Twin studies suggest that
genes explain only about
a quarter of the
differences in handedness.
The rest comes from
many small influences,
some of them before
we are born.
Conditions around birth
may play a role
too, although most
left-handers were born
without any complications.
So the hand you
write with may have
been taking shape long
before your first breath.
Why only one in
ten of us ends
up left-handed is a
longer story, and it
is waiting on Miya's Lab.
